reason: The support cells and connective fibers appear to be complementary parts of the skin's supporting layer.
expectation: They should form a supportive layer for the skin.

alternatives.reason: Joining neighboring surface cells also looks relevant to building the skin barrier.

effect: The fibers and support cells formed a skin layer that resists a sideways tug and includes capillaries. I can now build the surface barrier.
reaction: The tug illustration makes the layer's supporting role clear.
reason: Cell junctions bridge neighboring cells, so they look useful for joining the surface cells.
expectation: The junctions should join the surface cells into a more continuous layer.

effect: The junctions joined the surface cells, but water still escapes from the exposed layer.
reaction: The escaping water makes the remaining barrier problem clear.
reason: The tough outer layer has overlapping cells and lipids that appear suited to covering the moist surface.
expectation: The outer layer should cover the connected cells and reduce water loss.

effect: The outer layer reduced water loss and completed the surface barrier; it can now be joined to the supporting layer.
reaction: The comparison of water arrows makes the barrier's effect clear.
reason: The surface barrier and supporting skin layer appear to be complementary layers of the skin.
expectation: They should form a layered skin structure.

effect: The surface barrier and supporting layer formed layered skin, with vessels beneath the living surface cells. It still needs sensory endings to meet the goal.
reaction: The cross-section helps show how the layers relate.
reason: The sensory endings belong beneath the skin surface and should add contact sensing.
expectation: The endings should make the layered skin sensitive to contact.

effect: The skin now senses contact, but its nerve connection to the spinal cord is still open. The new goal also calls for a continuing supply.
reaction: The dashed gap makes the missing connection clear.
reason: The arm already has a connection to the nervous system, so adding the sensitive skin should connect touch information to it.
expectation: The skin should cover the arm and connect its touch signals to the nervous system.

effect: The skin now covers the arm and sends touch information to the spinal cord, but the supply connection remains open.
reaction: The separate insets make the completed nerve connection and missing supply clear.
reason: The body supply network carries oxygen and nutrients, which the skin-covered arm still needs.
expectation: The circulation should connect to the arm and supply its working tissues.

effect: The arm is now connected to circulation, and the new goal is to use contact feedback to hold the glass.
reaction: The separate nerve and blood-flow paths make their roles clear.
reason: The living body model has the hand and touch connection needed to interact with the glass.
expectation: The hand should hold the glass using contact feedback.

effect: The glass is held steady through a feedback loop: touch information reaches the nervous system, which sends commands to hand muscles. The final goal is complete.
reaction: The slipping-glass sequence makes the purpose of contact feedback concrete.

mostWorthwhile.text: Holding the glass was the most worthwhile moment because it brought touch, nerves and muscle work together in a recognizable situation.

leastWorthwhile.text: Joining the two skin layers was clear but less engaging on its own; its result mainly assembled pieces whose roles had already been introduced.

surprise.text: The connected surface cells still allowed water to escape; the outer layer and its lipids reduced that loss.

arbitrary.text: No action felt especially arbitrary. The item descriptions and goals gave a plausible reason for each combination.

continue.text: I would choose to continue if another chapter offered a similarly concrete problem. The glass sequence made the assembled systems feel useful, though several earlier combinations were predictable.
